source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Every state protects every apology, admission of fault and factual statement from evidence in exactly the same way in malpractice litigation.","B":"Apology laws prohibit clinicians from expressing sympathy after an adverse event because any compassionate statement is automatically an admission of negligence.","C":"Protections vary by jurisdiction and statement type; some laws protect expressions of sympathy, while admissions of fault may receive different or no protection.","D":"No U.S. jurisdiction addresses medical apologies or expressions of sympathy, so state law never affects disclosure communication after an adverse event."}}
source_row.rationale: Medical apology protections are jurisdiction-specific and statement-specific. Expressions of sympathy may be protected where admissions of fault are not, so clinicians should follow applicable state law and institutional disclosure policy.
source_row.source_detail: State-law summary and statute table show substantial variation: many jurisdictions exclude expressions of sympathy/condolence, while some extend or limit protection differently for admissions, fault or accompanying statements. National Conference of State Legislatures 50-state statutory summary, current page rechecked 2026-08-15; individual state law controls. Reviewed 2026-08-15.
source_row.stem: After an adverse event, a clinician wants to express sympathy or apologize. Which statement about U.S. medical apology laws is most accurate?
